[pAtl-i II

3. The subscribers to the memorandum of association and such other persons as the directors shall admit to membership shall be members of the company.

General Meetings

4. All general meetings other than annual general meetings shall be called extraordinary general meetings.

5. (1) The directors may, whenever they think fit, call an extraordinary general meeting.

(2) If at any time there are not within India directors capable of acting, who are sufficient in number to form a quorum, any director or any two members of the company may call an extraordinary general meeting in the same manner as nearly as possible, as that in which such a meeting may be called by the directors.

Proceedings at General Meetings

6. (1) No business shall be transacted at any general meeting unless a quorum of members is present at the time when the meeting proceeds to business.

(2) Save as herein otherwise provided, three members present in person shall be a quorum.

7. (1) If within half an hour from the time appointed for holding the meeting a quorum is not present, the meeting, if called upon the requisition of members, shall be dissolved.

(2) In any other case, the meeting shall stand adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place or to such other day and at such , other time and place as the directors may determine.

(3) If at the adjourned meeting a quorum is not present within half an hour from the time appointed for the meeting, the members present shall be a quorum.

8. The chairman, if any, of the board of directors shall preside as chairman at every general meeting of the company.

9. If there is no such chairman, or if he is not present within fifteen minutes after the time appointed for holding the meeting, or is unwilling to act as chairman of the meeting, the directors present shall elect one of their number to be chairman of the meeting.

10. If at any meeting no director is willing to act as chairman or if no director is present within fifteen minutes after the time appointed for holding the meeting, the members present shall choose one of their number to be chairman of the meeting.

11. (1) The chairman may, with the consent of any meeting at which a quorum is present and shall if so directed by the meeting, adjourn the meeting from time to time and from place to place.

(2) No business shall be transacted at any adjourned meeting other than the business left unfinished at the meeting from which the adjournment took place.

(3) When a meeting is adjourned for thirty days or more, notice of the adjourned meeting shall be given as in the case of an original meeting.

(4) Save as aforesaid, it shall not be necessary to give any notice of an adjournment or of the business to be transacted at an adjourned meeting. 12, In the case of an equality of votes, whether on a show of hands or on a poll, the chairman of the meeting at which the show of hands takes place, or at which the poll is demanded, shall be entitled to a second or casting vote.

13.- Any business other than that upon which a poll has been demanded may be proceeded with, pending the taking of the poll.

Votes of members

14. Every member shall have one vote.

15. A member of unsound mind, or in respect of whom an order has been made by any Court having jurisdiction in lunacy, may vote, whether on a show of hands or on a poll, by his committee or other legal guardian ,and any such committee or guardian may, on a poll, vote by proxy.

16. No member shall be entitled to vote at any general meeting unless all sums presently payable by him to the company have been paid.

17. (1) No objection shall be raised to the qualification of any voter except at the meeting or adjourned meeting at which the vote objected to is given or tendered, and every vote not disallowed at such meeting shall be valid for all purposes.

(2) Any such objection made in due time shall be referred to the chairman of the meeting, whose decision shall be final and conclusive.

18. A vote given in accordance with the terms of an instrument of proxy shall be valid notwithstanding the previous death or insanity of the principal or the revocation of the proxy or of the authority under which the proxy was executed, or the transfer of the shares in respect of which the proxy is given :

Provided that no intimation in writing of such death, inSanity, revocation or transfer shall have been received by the company at the office before the commencement of the meeting or adjourned meeting at which the proxy is used.

Directors

19. The number of the directors and the names of the first directors shall be determined in writing by the subscribers of the memorandum of association or a majority of them.

20. (i)The remuneration of the directors shall, in so far as it consists of a monthly payment, be deemed to accrue from day to day.

(2) The directois may also be paid all travelling, hotel and other expenses properly incurred by them—

(a) in attending and returning from meetings of the directors or any committee of the directors or general meetings of the company ; or

(b).in connection with the business of the company.

Proceedings of Meetings of Directors

21. (1) The directors may meet together for the despatch of business adjourn and otherwise regulate their meetings, as they think fit.

(2) A director may, and the managing agent, manager or secretary on the requisition of a director shall, at any time, summon a meeting of the directors.

22. (1) Questions arising at any meeting of the directors shall be decided by a majority of votes.

(2) In case of an equality of votes, the chairman shall have a second or casting vote.

23. The continuing directors may act notwithstanding any vacancy in their body; but, if and so long as their number is reduced below the quorum fixed by the Act for a meeting of directors, the continuing directors or director may act for the purpose of increasing the number of directors to that number, or of summoning a genera] meeting of the company, but for no other purpose.

24. (1) The directors may elect a chairman of their meetings and determine trie period for which he is to hold office.

(2) If no such chairman is elected, or if at any meeting the chairman is not present within five minutes after the time appointed for holding the meeting, the directors present may choose one of their number to be chairman of the meeting.

25. (1) The directors may, subject to the provisions of the Act, delegate any of their powers to committee consisting of such member or members of their body as they think fit.

(2) Any committee so formed shall, in the exercise of the powers so delegated, conform to any regulations that may be imposed on it by the directors.

26. (1) A committee may elect a chairman of its meetings.

(2) If no such chairman is elected, or if at any meeting the chairman is not present within five minutes after the time appointed for holding the meeting, the members present may choose one of their number to be chairman of the meeting.

27. (1) A committee may meet and adjourn as it thinks proper.

(2) Questions arising at any meeting of a committee shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present, and in case of an equality of votes, the chairman shall have a second or casting vote.

28. 29. The Seal.

Explanation I.—Where the managing agent is a firm, a change in its constitution means any change among the partners of the firm, not caused

(a) the death of a partner, or \Ji) the retirement of a partner on the expiry, by efflux of time, of his term of office as on the 21st day of July, 1951, or if he became a partner after that date, as fixed at the time when he became a partner, or

Explanation II.—Where the managing agent is a body corporate, a change in its constitution means—

(a) the conversion of the managing agent from a private to a public company or from a public to a private company, or

(b) any change among the directors or managers of the body corporate, not caused by—

(») the death of a director or manager ;

(in) 'he appointment of a new director or manager in the place of a director or manager who has died or has retired on the expiry of his term of office as aforesaid ; or

(c) save as provided in sub-section (2), any change in the registered ownership of shares in the corporation, or in the case of a corporation not having a share capital, any change in its membership, not caused by the death of any shareholder or member or his replacement by his heir.

(2) Where a managing agent is a public company, the shares whereof are for the time being dealt in, or quoted by, any of the recognised stock exchanges of India as notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette, no change in the registered ownership of the shares of the company shall be deemed to be a change in its constitution within the meaning and for the purposes of sub-section (1), unless the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, otherwise directs.

(3) No i-uch notification shall be is: ued in respect of any company unless the Central Government is of o; inion that any change in the registered ownership of its shares has taken place or is likely to take place, which has affected or is likily to affect prejudicially the affairs of any company which is being managed by the managing agent.

(4) Nothing in rub-section (1) thall apply to a private company unle s it is a sub idiary of a public company.

The Indian Companies (Amendment) Act, 1952. £TATFMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 1 be object of this Bill is to amend and consolidate the law relating to Companies. The last majcr emendment of the Indian Companies Act, 1913 (VII cf 1913) was undertaken in 1936 when the Indian Ccmpenies (Amendment) Act, 1936 (XXII of 1936) was passed. At the end cf Vi crld \\ zx II the need was felt for a further extensive revisicn cf the Ccnpfries Act. Apart from the experience gained of the actual vvcikirg cf the Anendment Act of 1936, which disclosed the necessity fcr sn eaily Eir.encment of some of its provisions, many changes had tsken place in the intervening years in the organisation and management of joirt stock companies, and c\er a wide sector that was dominated by new ekrr.er.ts in lixde end industry, the character of company management had alsc n ateriaU> &ltered. Further, at the end of the War, the Company Law Amendment Ccn irittee in the United Kingdom, more familiarly known as the Cohen Ccnnittec, had submitted its Repcrt after a laborious enquiry spreec' c\er twe veais. Ihis Repcrt recemmended several far-reaching charges in tie Irtish Companies Act, 1929. As the Indian company law had Lten ahujs largely based on the prevailing English law, the then Gc\eirn ent felt trrt the urne was ripe fcr a further review of the Indian Ccr. rtnieE Act A geed deal of ejiplcrator} work was done between 1946 n d 1950. Tv.c distinguished company lawyers were successively appointed to revise Cc\cirn ent en the bread lines on which the Indian Companies Act shculd be revised. The recemmendations of these two lawyers were firther e>£irircd in the then Ministry of Commerce, and certain tentative departmental views which emerged were circulated in a memorandum to the cereiel pullic fcr eliciting opinion on them. Many representations en tl is rrtrrcrEr.ci.n-1 were duly received from trade and industrial organisation, learned bedies, associations, State Governments and the general puliiu At tr e end cf 195c, the Government of India appointed a Committee under the chaiirrsnship cf Shri C. H. Bhabha to go into the entire question cf the revision cf the Indian Companies Act, w;th particular reference to its beerirg en the development cf Indian trade and industry. This Committee exerrined a large number of witnesses in different parts of the country and submitted its Pepcrt in March 1952. The Repcrt was circulated to all State Gc\ err merits. Chambers of Commerce, many trade associations and several learned bedies for an expression of their views on the recommendations contained in it, A special officer was also appointed in the Department cf Eccrcn'ic Affairs at the same time to examine the Report and, en the tfsis cf the views expressed by these organised trade and other associations and tire general public, to submit proposals to Government for the revision of the Indian Companies Act.

2. The present Bill is based largely on the recommendations of the Ccmpeny Law Committee modified in a few particulars by the views expressed on these recommendations. The main principles underlying these recomtnendatiors are as follows :

(i) the provisions of the law both in regard to the formation and management cf joint stock companies should be such as would ensure the maintenance of a minimum standard of good behaviour in ccn pany prcmotion and management without imposing needlessly irkscme or rigid rules which may hamper legitimate business or affect initiative or enterprise ;

(ii) the law should provide fcr the fullest possible disclosure in prospectuses or statements in lieu cfpiospectuces r-sued both before

THE GAZETTE OF 'INDIA EXTRAORDINARY and after a company is formed, and failure to make such disclosure should be visited with effective penalties ;

(iii) company accounts should be prepared in such a way as to disclose all facts which are material to a full understanding of the manner in which companies are worked ;

(iv) company meetings should be called and conducted in such a way as to ens-ure that shareholders receive all reasonable facilities for exercising an intelligent judgment on the activities of the management ;

(v) the provisions for investigation into the affairs of a company should be so designed as to enable an appropriate authority to intervene in its affairs not merely when an offence has been committed, but also when it is established that the affairs of a company are being managed in a manner prejudicial to the shareholders of the company or oppressive to any substantial portion of them or when such investigation is otherwise necessary in the public interest ;

(vi) the law should also provide for the establishment of an appropriate authority not merely for enforcing the provisions of the Companies Act or for carrying out the investigations which may be necessary under it, but also for generally overseeing the administration of the Act and for exercising in the public interest that reserve of authority which must necessarily vest in some organ of Government, The provisions of the Bill in its different Parts follow largely from the above principles. The major changes in the present Indian Companies Act wHch the Eill introduces thus relate to the following topics :

(a) the promotion and formation of companies (clauses 50 to 74) ;

(b) the capital structure of companies (clauses 79 to 83) ;

(c) company meetings and procedure (clauses 158 to 189) ;

(d) the presentation of company accounts, their audit, and the powers and duties of auditors (clauses 195 to 218) ;

(e) the inspection and investigation of the affairs companies (clauses 219 to 235) ;

(f) the cccstitution of boards of directors, and the powers and duties of directors, managing directors and managers (clauses 236 to

(g) the appointment of managing agents, terms and conditions of their service, their remuneration, the powers of managing agents vis-a-vis directors, and the activities of managing agents in regard to borrowings, loans, contracts, sales and purchases (clauses 307 to 359) ; and

(h) the administration of company law.

Most of the new provisions contained in the Bill on all these points are self-explanatory, and in the case of almost all these provisions the relevant notes on clauses have indicated the recommendations of the Company Law Committee on which they are based.

[PART I

3. As has been already mentioned, jn a few particulars, the provisions of the Bill have deviated from the recommendations of the Company Law Committee. These deviations are, however, of a minor nature, and the notes on clauses have duly indicated and explained them. There is, however, one important deviation from the recommendations of the Company Law Committee which needs special mention. The Company Law Committee devoted a good deal of space in its Report to problems of organisation, and administration, and recommended that the Central Government should not only resume its responsibility for the administration of joint stock companies which it had delegated to the State Governments, but that a statutory authoity at the Centre, to be called " Corporate Investment and Administration Commisskn ", should be set up under the new Act for the administration of the company law as well as for the discharge of other related functions, e.g. capital issue control and regulation of stock exchanges when a Central measure for this latter purpose was passed.

Action has already been taken on the first recommendation of the Company Law Committee. The State Governments have been addressed regarding the intention of the Central Government to resume its powers under the Indian Companies Act and the constitution of a Central Organiation under the administrative control of the Department of Economic Affairs has been sanctioned. It is, however, proposed that the question of conferring statutory status on this Organisation, if so necessary, may be considered after this Central Organisation has been set up and functioned for a reasonable period. For present therefore the duties and responsibilities which the Company Law Committee visualised for the statutory authority would be carried on by the new deparimental organisation.

In the light of the recent experience of the Central Government, provision has also been made in the Bill in respect of one or two matters which were not covered by the recommendations of the Company Law Committee but which are considered to be of sufficient importance to the working of joint stock companies in future to justify the making of special provisions in regard to them (e.g. clause 366). The notes on the relevant clauses will explain the reasons for these provisions. 4, _ It is necessary to draw attention in this context to two other recommendations of the Company Law Committee which have affected the structure of the Bill. In the Indian Companies (Amendment) Act, 1951 (LU of 1951), certain specia 1 powers were conferred on Courts of Law and the Central Government. While the powers conferred on the Courts by section 7 of that Act were based largely on the provisions of section 210 of the English Companies Act, 1948, the other powers conferred on the Central.

Government were of a quasl-administrativc nature to be exercised on the recommendations of an Advisory Commission provided for under section 8 of the Amendment Act. The Company Law Committee recommended that if and when the Indian Companies Act was comprehensively revised on the lines of its recommendations, Government should consider the desirability of repealing sections 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 of the Amendment Act of 1951 conuinhig these quasi-administrative powers. While it is not proposed to retainindefinitely these special powers, which the Central Government assumed in 1951, it is considered that it willnot be expedient for the Central Government in the present circumstances of company management in this country, to divest itself of these powers till experience of the working of the new Act has shown that these special powers are no longer necessary. Clause 598 of the Bill, therefore, proposes the retention of these powers for a period of three years from the commencment of the new Act. The provisionf cf sections.

2. 3. 4. 5. 6 and 8 of tha \m:ndmjnt Act of 1951, which have been, incorporated in the present Indian Companies Act as sections 86J, 87AA 87B [second proviso to clause (c)], 87BB, 87 CG and 239B, have therefore been relegated to a Schedule (Schedule XI) attached to this Bill. Section 7 of the Amendment Act, which it is proposed to incorporate permanently in the Companies Act, has been retained as clauses 367 to 377. The notes on these clauses explain these structural changes.

In regard to Table A in the pressnt Act, the Company Law Committee recommended that having regard to the importance of the provisions contained in the compulsory regulations of this Table, it was desirable that they should be inserted as independent sections in the Act itself. The acceptance of this recommendation has involved the transfer to the body of the Bill of many of the provisions hitherto included in Table A. Further, in order to avoid unnecessary duplication, those regulations in Table A which merely draw attention to the relevant provisions of the Act have been omitted. In the result the new Table A has been considerably abridged. The notes on clauses relating to this Table explain these structural alterations •

5. Advantage has been taken of the opportunity offered tor the consolidation of the Act for the first time since 1913 to re-arrange its different Parts in a more logical order. The general principle has been to arrange the different Parts of the Act in such a way that they follow, as far as possible, the chronological sequence in the formation, growth and decay of companies. Thus, for example, it has been felt that the provisions of the Act which relate to the formation of companies should precede those relating to their management. The re-arrangement of matter which has followed as a consequence of this decision has entail;d considerable changes in the structure of the present Act. It is, however, felt that these changes will eventually result in a better understanding and appreciation of the scheme of theIndian Companies Act.

C D . DESHMUKH, NEW DELHI ;

The 22nd August, 1953.

Clause 3.—This combines clauses (2), (7), (13) and (13A) of sub-section

(1) of section 2 and section 2A of the existing Act. The Acts enumerated in clause 3(i)(ii) are previous companies laws. Proviso (i) to section 2A of the existing Act has become spent and has therefore been omitted.

Clause 4.—As suggested by the Company Law Committee (paragraph 27), the definitions are based on those found in section 154 of the English Act.

The illustration has been added so as to bring out clearly the intention underlying sub-clause (i)(c). A few minor drafting improvements have also been effected.

Clause 5.—This is based on section 440(2) of the English Act.

The language, however, has been amplified so as to cover all cases which are intended to be included.

For instance, a person who is himself guilty of the default, failure etc., although he cannot be said to authorise or permit the default or failure is obviously intended to be within the scope of this provision.

Clause 6.—This is based on section 455(2) of the English Act, vide paragraph 30 of the Company Law Committee's Report.

Clause 7.—This is intended to make it clear that the provisions of this Bill will override the memorandum, articles, agreements executed by the company, and resolutions passed in general meeting by the company and resolutions passed by the directors of the company, unless it is expressy provided otherwise in the Bill itself. This clause will apply whether the memorandum or articles, agreements or resolutions, be before or after coming into operation of this Bill.

Clause 8.—This is based on the recommendation made by the Company Law Committee in paragraph 31 of its Report.

In regard to winding up> the District Court may be invested with jurisdiction only in respect of companies whose paid-up share capital is one lakh of rupees or less. respect of certain other specified matters chief among which are those relating to investigation, and remedial action where the company acts either oppressively, or prejudicially to the interests of the company, jurisdiction will vest exclusively in the High Court.

Sub-clause (3) provides for the exemption of any company or class of companies from compliance with the requirements laid down in the Bill if in the opinion of the Central Government the grant of exemption is necessary in the national interest.

Sub-clause (5) (»') and (it) contains a special provision in regard to banking companies and insurance companies. Those companies, by reason of the non-disclosure of any matters which are exempted from disclosure by virtue of the Banking Companies Act or the Insurance Act, should not be regarded as not disclosing their true and fair view of the affairs.

Sub-clause (5) (iii) makes the same provision in the case of other companies which have been exempted from giving information either by virtue of Schedule VI of the Bill or by virtue of a notification or order issued under sub-clause (3) or sub-clause (4) of this clause.

Clause 241.—clearly affirms the right of a person to be appointed as director, provided the requisite notice of the intention to stand, or propose him as a candidate is given. This clause will prevent provisions being inserted in the articles, placing restrictions other than those laid down in the Bill in the case of public companies or private companies which are subsidiary of public companies.

Clause 242.—This is based on regulation 83 in Table A of the existing Act.

Clause 243.—This is based on the recommendations of the Company Law Committee and the provisions of sub-section (2) (in) of new section 83B at pages 356 and 357 of the Report. The Company Law Committee recommended that there should be a majority of not less than 80 percent before the persons who are connected with the managing agent in the manner specified in this clause are appointed directors in vacancies which are subject to retirement by annual rotation. It is considered that a special resolution, that is to say, a resolution passed by not less than three-fourths of the votes cast at a meeting will suffice in this case also. The Bill requires a special resolution in various places and there is no special reason to distinguish this case from those cases. The exceptions contained in the provisos to paragraphs (a) and (j) of sub-clause (1) are obviously necessary.

Clause 248.—See the recommendation of the Company Law Committee in paragraph 86 of its Report, and also section 182 of the English Act. The recommendation of the Company Law Committee that the qualifying shares should be held beneficially by a director may lead to difficulties in practice. Such a requirement is not imposed by the English Act. It is therefore considered desirable to omit that requirement.

Where the requisite shares are held in the name of a person, it seems unnecessary to gobehind that fact and enquire whether he holds the share solely and beneficially for himself. Sub-section (2) of the redraft of section 85 suggested at page 358 of the Company Law Committee Report has therefore been omitted.

Sub-clause (4) corresponds to section 86 1(2) of the existing Act. It is considered necessary, to confine the power of a company to add to the disqualifications imposed by the Bill to private companies which are not subsidiaries of public companies.

Clause 253 to 257.—These limit the number of directorships which may be held by a single individual to twenty. Sec paragraph 91 of the Company Law Committee's Report and the draft suggested by the Committee at page 359, That draft hn been split up and amplified so as to make clear provision for all the cases which may arise.

Clauses 258 to 269.—These impose an age limit on directors, but subject to the right of the company to override it.

See paragraph 90 of the Company Law Committee's Report and the summary of the recommendations at page 254 of the Report which impose a rigid and inflexible age limit.

It is not however considered desirable to go beyond the provisions of the English Act (section 185) and impose an absolute disqualification on persons who have attained the age of 65. If a company, having been specifically made aware of the age of a director, chooses to appoint him or to declare that he should not retire in virtue of the age limit, it is considered that it isbetter to permit it to have its way.

The provisions contained in these clauses arc otherwise closely modelled on the provisions of sections 185 and 186 of the English Act. As in those sections, it will be open to the company by its articles to imposes a lower age limit than 65 if it so chooses.

The English Act Sub-clause (2) is a consequential provision, which seems to be clearly necessary- Sub-clause

(3) corresponds to sub-section (2) of the existing section 86 1 but confines the operation of the sub-section to private companies which are not subsidiaries of public companies.

The clause gives a reasonable measure of protection to lenders who have acted in ignorance of the fact that the restrictions imposed on the Company by the clause have not been observed. See regulation 70 of Table A of the English Act.

Clause 273.—See paragraph 106, and the redraft of Section 86D at page 362, of the Company Law Committee's Report. Clause (iv) of sub-section (1) of the redraft has been split up into two. Where the directors control the exercise of not less than 50 percent of the total voting power of a public company, the prohibition will apply automatically. In other cases, that is, where the directors control less than 50 percent of the total voting power, it will be open to the Government to declare that the directors have vsufficient control over the company to make the application of the clause reasonable in the circumstances of the case.

Clause 274.—The mere fact that for the purpose of the balance sheet, a book debt is required to be treated as a loan or an advance should not make the provisions of clause 273 applicable, unless it is clear that the transaction represented by the book credit was, from the very inception in the nature of a loan or an advance.

In such cases, within the limit laid down out.,-that the value of the goods or materials involved should not exceed Rs. 1,000 in one calendar year, the clauses will not apply. Where the requisite consent is not accorded the contact will be voidable at the option of the directors.

Clause 340.—This piovides for a managing agent or an associate of the ntnagirig agent receiving commission in special circumstances where he is

THE GAZETTE OF INDlA EXTRAORDINARY appointed a buying agent of the company. The Company Law Committee has recommended that no commission need be paid for purchases made by a managing agent on behalf of a company, but it is well known that in cases where a managing agent managing several companies makes bulk purchases for fulfilling the needs of all the companies considerable economies result' and it is clearly desirable that in such cases the managing agent should be entitled at least to the outlay which he has had to incur.

The clause therefore provides for the vesting of a discretion in the company to allow reimbursement or a commission in cases where purchases are made by the managing agent outside the State in which the goods purchased are to be used, provided the managing agent or associate maintains an office at that place for his own business.

SEC. 21 Clause 366.—This is a new provision and it is intended to provide, at the instance of the Government, for the amalgamation of two or more companies in the national interest. Occasionally, cases arise where such an amalgamation in the national interest is clearly a necessity. The observance of the usual procedure prescribed by the existing Act in such cases will lead to prolonged delays which will be detrimental to the national interest. It has been made clear that any order made by the Government should provide for the old share holders, and the old debenture holders and other creditors, having the same interest in the company resulting from the amalgamation as they had in the original companies. Any order made by the Government under this clause will be laid on the table of both Houses of Parliament and will therefore be subject to the Parliamentary scrutiny.

Clauses 398 to 401.—These are intended to give effect to the recom mendations in paragraph 207 of the Company Law Committee's Report Compare sections 218, 219 and 220 of the English Act. The effect of these clauses will be as follows :

(1) The High Court will have jurisdiction to transfer any case to a District Court.

(2) Proceedings instituted in a District Court in pursuance of the jurisdiction conferred upon it by virtue of clause 9 of the Bill may be transferred by the High Court either to its own file or [to the file of some other District Court.

(3) The High Court may direct that proceedings may continue in any Dirtrict Court although that District Court might not have had jurisdiction to receive the petition in the first instance.

(4) Orders may be passed by the High Court at any time or at any stage and whether an application in regard to the matters has been presented by a party or not.

Clause 572.—This confers in general the power on the Central Government to reduce any fee, charge, or other sum specified in the Act as payable to the Central Government.

Clause 573.—Corresponds to section 249A of the existing Indian Act and section 428 of the English Act.

Clause 574.—Incorporates the provision contained in section 287 of the Indian Act. It makes it clear that insurance and other companies which are governed by special Acts will continue to be governed by those Acts and that such companies will be governed by the provisions of the bill in so far as those provisions are not in consistent with those contained in the special Acts governing those companies.

Clause 575.—This is intended to give power to the Central Government to modify the application of the Act where the shares or the predominant interest is held by the Central or a State Government or by two or more of those Governments. It is only where the interest held by the Government or Governments concerned is J ths or more of the total paid up share capital of the company that this provisions of this clause can be invoked.

Clause 576.—Corresponds to section 289A of the existing Act.

Clause 577.—This is based on the redraft of section 278(1) in pursuance of paragraphs 203 and 233 of the Company Law Committee's Report Which is to be found at pages 441 to 442 of the Report.

Clause 579.—Corresponds to sub-section (3) of the redraft mentioned above.

Clause 580.—Corresponds to sub-section (4) of the redraft mentioned above.

Clause 581.—This embodies sub-sections (5) to (11) of the redraft referred to above. This is intended to safeguard directors and other officers of the companies from frivolous or vexations attacks in criminal cases. The principal change is that the compensation which may be awarded has been raised from Rs. 250 provided for in the Civil Procedure Code to Rs. 5,000. The imprisonment which may be ordered in default of payment has been enhanced from one to six months.

Clause 582.—This is intended to give effect to the recommendations of the Company Law Committee in paragraph 191 of the Report. See also page 308.

Clause 583.—This corresponds to section 279 of the existing Act and 444 of the English Act.

Clause 584.—This corresponds to section 441 of the English Act the application of which is recommended in paragraph 234 of the Company Law Committee's Report.

Clause 585.—Corresponds to section 282 of the Indian Act and section 438 of the English Act.

Clause 586.—Corresponds to section 238 of the Indian Act. It is rl ar that the provisions of that section should not be confined to false evidence in winding-up proceedings but should extend generally to false evidence given in all proceeding under the Bill.

Clause 587.—Corresponds to section 282A of the existing Act, Clause 588.-—Corresponds to section 283 of the Indian Act and section 439 of the English Act.

Clause 589,—corresponds to section 280 of the Indian and section 447 of the English Act.

Clause 590.—corresponds to section 281 of the Indian and section 444 of the English Act.

Clause 591.—This enables the company to reduce any fee, charges, etc. payable to it by virtue of the provisions of the Bill or of the provisions contained in the articles governing the company. In a number of places reference is made in the existing Act to a specific fee with power to the company to reduce the amount of the fee. The insertion of this clause makes it unnecessary to refer to the power of the company to reduce the fee, charges, etc., in various places in the Bill.

Clause 592.—This provides for the delegation by the Central Government of its power and functions under the Act. The Company Law Committee recommended the creation of a Central Authority in which various powers should be vested. This will enable the Government to implement this recommendation as soon as the time is ripe for doing so.

Clause 503.—This is based on the recommendation of the Company Law Committee that there should be an Annual Report. See paragraph 262 and page 337 of the Company Law Committee's Report. The corresponding section of the English Act is section 451.

Clause 594.—This corresponds to section 151(2) and (3) of the existing Act and section 454 of the English Act. Power has been taken in general terms to alter or add to all the schedules except schedules XI and XII.

Clause 505.—This is based on section 151(1) of the Indian Act and section 454 of the English Act.

Clause 596.—This is based on section 151(4) and (5) of the existing Indian Act.

Clause 597.—This is largely based on section 246 of the existing Indian Act. Having regard to the fact that the rule-making power will be conferred not only in regard to matters relating to the winding up of a company but also in regard to other matters, e.g., those concerned with the approval of terms with creditors and members, the reduction of share capital, the subdivision of shares, etc., the appropriate place for this provision will not bo in Part VII which deals only with the winding up of the companies but in the General Part, vie; Part XIII.

Clause 598.—This provides for the continuance of such of the provisions of the amending Act (L II of 1951) as have not been incorporated in the Bill. The power conferred by section 7 of that Act with regard to giving power to the Court to act when a company acts either prejudicially to its own interest or practises oppression of any of its member or members, have teen embodied in clauses 367-377 of the Bill. The other provisions giving powers of control to the Government in respect of the appointment, reappointment, etc., of the directors, managing agents and the like, contained in sections 2 to 6 of the amending Act, providing for the constitution of a commission to advise the Government on the matters referred to in those sections (section 8) were not intended to have permanent application but only to deal with what is believed to be a transitional phase in the management of the companies in this country. These provisions, therefore., stand repealed.

SCHEDULE I TABLE B This embodies only the provisions in the existing Table B. Slight drafting improvements have been made. It will be open to the Government to alter the fees prescribed by the list in pursuance of the power conferred on them by clause 594 of the Bill.

SCHEDULE II This corresponds to the Fourth Schedule of the English Act. Some slight alterations and amplifications suggested by the Company Law Committee in the redraft of the Schedule at pages 390 to 398 of the Report have also been embodied.

SCHEDULE III This corresponds to the Fifth Schedule of the English Act. The provisions contained in that Schedule have been incorporated wih some additions end alterations here and there,

SCHEDULE IV This corresponds to the Third Schedule of the English Act. Some additions and alteration have been made.

SCHEDULE V This corresponds to the Sixth Schedule of the English Act. It has been made clear that the annual return should relate to the date of the last annual general meeting. No other changes of substance have been made.

SCHEDULE VI—PART I This is mostly based on the Company Law Committee's draft Balance Sheet at pages 408 to 416 of the Report. The alterations made are not substantial and are only intended to give effect to the intention of the Company Law Committee in as clear terms as possible. When any assets are written up in a balance sheet, the amount of the increase will have to be noted in the balance sheets for subsequent five years instead of for three subsequent years.

This alteration has been made in order to make the provision uniform with that which will apply where the assets are written down.

SCHEDULE VI—PART II This is also based on the form suggested by the Company Law Committee at pages 417 to 420 of the Report. Here again nothing has been changed except for a few minor drafting improvements, which are intended to make the position as clear as possible.

The managing agent, in addition to the specific powers mentioned by the Company Law Committee will also have all powers which may be lawfully delegated to him by the directors. This is in accordance with the intention of the Company Law Committee.
